title: Flowers of Home, the Sky Is Too Narrow for My Mouth
intro: In exile, Ihab al-Shabatat asks the flowers at home what has happened to his power of speech. He remembers a woman passing close enough for him to see the dust rise at her anklet, yet he cannot find a word to address her. The language shifts from honey, moonlight and magic to the blood cells in his own veins, before dawn finds him still grieving.

translation: Flowers of home, the sky is too narrow for my mouth.
Give me a hand, let me see what has befallen it.
1.sharh: He has more to say than even the sky can hold, yet something is wrong with his mouth. The first intelligible answer will come from flowers.

translation: In the whisper of dew the flowers answered,
“The image of a loved one gone.” I said, “Perhaps.”
2.sharh: Dew gives the flowers the faintest of voices. They diagnose an absent beloved's image, but his “perhaps” leaves room for the rest of the poem to test their answer.

translation: Love groans when a heart yearns for its beloved.
It tastes the bitter gourd and finds it honey.
3.sharh: Love changes the very sense that ought to distinguish one taste from another. Something as bitter as colocynth tastes like honey to the person who longs for it.

translation: Night follows night as I try to forget in exile.
My longing sits with me, still singing.
4.sharh: Forgetting would require a little quiet. Longing has taken the empty seat beside the exile and keeps him company with a song.

translation: A full moon rises high, only to fade
before my loved one's image. Longing was my ladder.
5.sharh: He reaches the moon by climbing his own longing. Once the absent face is set beside it, even the full moon looks dim.

translation: Visions of love swept the young man towards a passion
where he sees his own death as dream and prize.
6.sharh: The young lover imagines himself coming away with a prize. What he is ready to count as a gain is the loss of his very self.

translation: Whoever has never tasted love's humiliation, in his ignorance,
takes death for play and this wound for balm.
7.sharh: From outside the experience it is easy to mistake the wound itself for a remedy. That mistake follows the lover's equally strange accounting of loss and gain.

translation: God folded away the years whose embers I grasped,
as though love were my faith and I came submitting to it.
8.sharh: The years have been put away, but he remembers how they burned his hand. “Submitting” can also name the Muslim, giving a religious force to his fidelity.

translation: My glances are fluent in the language of Western eyes.
Before Arab women my heart loses its speech.
9.sharh: His eyes can converse readily with Western eyes. In front of women who speak his own language it is the heart itself that becomes inarticulate.

translation: With medicine the beauties of the West look natural.
Eastern magic exposes them as dolls.
10.sharh: The geographical comparison belongs to the enamoured speaker. He imagines medicine producing a natural appearance, while the unaccountable pull he calls magic makes the artifice visible.

translation: Sons of my people, your daughters are forbidden to me.
Their eyes deem killing hearts an act of generosity.
11.sharh: He declares himself barred from the very women whose glances undo him. What their eyes dispense so generously is the fatal wound of love poetry.

translation: I am slain by love for women who withhold tenderness.
My name fares like my heart. They begrudge us their mercy.
12.sharh: The women grant no mercy to a man whose heart is all giving. The mention of his own name gains point from Ihab, a name associated in Arabic with giving.

translation: I remembered you, tears filling my pillows,
night my covering when I could bear secrecy no longer.
13.sharh: He has made an entire bed out of what he conceals. Tears take the place of the stuffing and darkness supplies the cover.

translation: Does every pursuit earn its pursuer praise?
How, when she passed in a breath of perfume?
14.sharh: The question about pursuing someone gives way to a sensation that comes unbidden. She has scarcely passed before he finds himself breathing her in.

translation: I made my approach. My thoughts of her were not hers.
She rose beyond my sight and came down frowning.
15.sharh: Approaching her reveals the distance between his expectations and hers. His gaze raises her high, but what comes back down to him is a frown.

translation: Whoever consults his mind just after his tongue
finds disapproval writ in people's eyes.
16.sharh: He has consulted the right adviser a moment too late, after the words are out. The faces around him supply the judgement he should have sought beforehand.

translation: She walked ahead of me, behind those fluttering steps.
My heart stood still with me and nearly spoke.
17.sharh: Everything moves except him. A heart that has nearly stopped with emotion is also, paradoxically, the one part of him that comes close to speaking.

translation: I held back my hand, my eye the shadow of her image.
My mouth faltered. My heart recalled a dictionary.
18.sharh: He restrains his hand and watches even her shadow. His heart holds a whole dictionary, yet his mouth cannot produce a word.

translation: In her haste her anklet drew close to the dust.
The earth flew above me, and I watched for stars.
19.sharh: All he sees at first is the anklet near the ground. Her passing throws up a sky's worth of dust, turning his gaze from her feet towards stars.

translation: White doves circle the growth in her wake.
Through it the earth nearly brings Jurhum back to life.
20.sharh: Her footprints seem to leave enough growing life to attract a flock of doves. Naming the ancient tribe of Jurhum makes a single footfall reach back across generations.

translation: Her pupils appeared as night, and so did her hair.
Yet night, as far as I knew, never had a twin.
21.sharh: The darkness of her pupils and her hair gives him two nights at once. For a moment what he knows about the beauty in front of him contradicts what he knows about the sky.

translation: Babylon's spells took human form in her.
My poetic demon made pilgrimage to her to learn.
22.sharh: Babylon evokes an old seat of magic. In Arabic lore a poet might have a jinn who inspired his verses. Here even that supposed teacher must become her pupil.

translation: One thought from her revives a dead mind,
and she extinguishes a living heart made captive by love.
23.sharh: A thought of her is enough to revive the faculty that makes poems. The heart on which the poems depend may be undone by the very same encounter.

translation: She has a die in my heart, faced with the faces of time.
It shows me time's frown when I land a smile.
24.sharh: The “faces” belong both to a die and to fortune. Even when the throw seems to yield a smiling mouth, the face time turns towards him frowns.

translation: When I smile, other people are mirrors for it.
I think I see myself there. I was a fancy.
25.sharh: From the changing faces of the die he turns to human faces. Trying to recover his own smile in them makes him wonder how much of the self he sees is imagined.

translation: Time spins its millstone faster through my youth.
Tomorrow turns to yesterday as I step forward again.
26.sharh: Again the figure is something that turns, now a mill. A step meant to bring him into the future discovers that the future has already been ground into the past.

translation: She has a nightly observance in my vein. If I neglect it,
the cells rise up, imagining infection.
27.sharh: Warid, a vein, and wird, a regularly repeated devotion, almost echo each other in Arabic. His body treats a missed night of remembrance as though an infection had entered the blood.

translation: The white cells' blades rise over their red sister.
Every vision is black when it draws near blindness.
28.sharh: The studio gloss identifies the two sisters as white and red blood cells. A disturbance inside the body becomes a battle of colours, until the eye can see only black.

translation: By night her spirit wrapped itself in my tears.
I bear the blame. The one who returned was no Mary.
29.sharh: Her presence returns under cover of night but is visible in his eyes. Mary enters the line at the point of return and reproach, recalling her return to face her people in the Quran.

translation: If morning comes to me with a night traveller's lamp,
we both weep for ourselves. Time has become a wake.
30.sharh: Dawn ought to make a lamp unnecessary. Arriving like another traveller still out after dark, it sees the same scene as the lover, and the two join in mourning.

1.1.7.head: السَّماء
1.1.7.meaning: The sky. The poet shortens sama' to sama for the metre.

3.2.3.head: شَهد
3.2.3.meaning: Honey, especially honey in the comb.

4.1.4.meaning: The effort of putting something out of mind.

5.2.3.head: الجَوى
5.2.3.meaning: The inward ache of passionate love.

6.1.5.head: مَغرَم
6.1.5.meaning: An absorbing passion, from a root also used of an inescapable debt.

7.2.6.head: بَلسَم
7.2.6.meaning: Balm, a soothing substance applied to a wound.

9.1.2.head: رومِيّات
9.1.2.meaning: Western women in this comparison. The historical name Rum denotes the Romans or Byzantines.

9.2.4.head: تَعَجَّمَ
9.2.4.meaning: To lose one's powers of speech or become unintelligible.

10.2.5.head: دُميَة
10.2.5.meaning: Dolls or figurines fashioned in human form.

13.1.3.head: حَشو
13.1.3.meaning: The stuffing or filling of something soft.

14.1.2.head: مُساعاة
14.1.2.meaning: An endeavour or pursuit, here making an approach to the woman.

14.2.1.head: كَيف
14.2.1.meaning: “Then how?” The recording asks a question here. In his published text he instead swears by the woman who passes.

16.1.2.head: اِستَخارَ
16.1.2.meaning: To seek guidance in choosing. He consults his mind only after speaking.

16.2.5.head: نُكراء
16.2.5.meaning: Something objectionable or alarming, here the disapproval in people's eyes.

17.1.4.head: واجِفَة
17.1.4.meaning: Hurrying or trembling, a word used of both movement and the heart.

19.1.1.head: خَلخال
19.1.1.meaning: An anklet worn close to the ground.

19.2.2.meaning: Earth or soil, originally damp soil.

20.2.6.head: جُرهُم
20.2.6.meaning: Jurhum, an ancient Arab tribe associated in tradition with Mecca and Ishmael.

22.1.3.head: بابِل
22.1.3.meaning: Babylon, an ancient city in Iraq associated with magic in Arabic tradition.

22.2.3-4.head: شَيطان الشِّعر
22.2.3-4.meaning: “The demon of poetry”, the jinn imagined in Arabic poetic lore to inspire a poet.

24.1.5.head: نَرد
24.1.5.meaning: A die whose throw turns up one of its faces.

24.2.6.head: مَبسِم
24.2.6.meaning: A smiling mouth or the place where a smile appears.

27.1.4.head: وِرد
27.1.4.meaning: A regularly repeated portion of prayer or recitation.

27.2.5.head: تَجَرثُم
27.2.5.meaning: Microbial infection, a term from modern medicine.

28.1.2.head: ظُبَة
28.1.2.meaning: The keen edges or tips of blades.

28.1.3-4.head: البَيضاء وَالحَمراء
28.1.3-4.meaning: “The white and the red”, the blood cells identified in the studio's gloss.

29.2.6.head: مَريَم
29.2.6.meaning: Mary, mother of Jesus, who returns to her people bearing her child in Quran 19.

30.1.5.head: مُدلِج
30.1.5.meaning: A traveller who makes a journey by night.
